bill.latestActionText: Referred to the Committee on Energy and Commerce, and in addition to the Committee on Ways and Means, for a period to be subsequently determined by the Speaker, in each case for consideration of such provisions as fall within the jurisdiction of the committee concerned.
subjects: Department of Health and Human Services

industries.rationale: The bill would reverse requirements affecting health insurers' enrollment processes, eligibility verification obligations, and coverage mandates for essential health benefits.
Changes to marketplace enrollment periods and coverage of certain procedures would affect patient volume and reimbursement for hospitals and physician groups.

bill.plainSummary: This resolution would block a federal rule issued in June 2025 that changes how people enroll in health insurance through the Affordable Care Act marketplaces. The rule sets new enrollment deadlines, requires more identity checks for certain applicants, bars people with DACA status from using the marketplaces, and prevents insurers from covering certain medical procedures as essential benefits. If passed, the resolution would nullify these changes and leave prior rules in place.

plain.whoItTouches: Anyone who buys health insurance. Anyone who pays a medical bill.

bill.title: Medicare Hearing Aid Coverage Act of 2025
bill.latestActionText: Referred to the Committee on Energy and Commerce, and in addition to the Committee on Ways and Means, for a period to be subsequently determined by the Speaker, in each case for consideration of such provisions as fall within the jurisdiction of the committee concerned.

industries.rationale: Medical device manufacturers that produce hearing aids would gain a new Medicare reimbursement market.
Audiologists and other providers conducting hearing examinations would receive Medicare payment for services currently not covered.
Medicare Advantage plans and supplemental insurers would face new coverage obligations and cost structures for hearing aids.

bill.plainSummary: This bill would expand Medicare to cover hearing aids and the examinations needed to fit them. Currently, Medicare does not pay for hearing aids. The bill also directs the Government Accountability Office to study existing programs that help people with hearing loss obtain hearing aids and related services.

It would also formally cover services provided by respiratory therapists, require a standardized electronic prescription form, and give patients specific rights such as choosing their own oxygen supplier.

bill.title: To amend the War Powers Resolution to provide for the limitation on Federal funding in contravention of the requirements of the War Powers Resolution.
bill.latestActionText: Referred to the Committee on Foreign Affairs, and in addition to the Committee on Armed Services, for a period to be subsequently determined by the Speaker, in each case for consideration of such provisions as fall within the jurisdiction of the committee concerned.

industries.rationale: Funding restrictions tied to War Powers compliance could directly affect defense contractors' revenue streams from military operations and deployments.

bill.plainSummary: This bill would amend the War Powers Resolution to restrict federal funding for military actions that do not comply with the War Powers Resolution's requirements. The War Powers Resolution currently governs when and how the President must seek congressional authorization for military operations. The bill appears to add a funding enforcement mechanism to those existing requirements, though the text provided does not specify the details of how the funding limitation would work.

bill.title: No WAR Act
bill.latestActionText: Referred to the Committee on Rules, and in addition to the Committee on the Budget, for a period to be subsequently determined by the Speaker, in each case for consideration of such provisions as fall within the jurisdiction of the committee concerned.

industries.rationale: The bill directly affects the procedural pathway for authorizing and funding military operations, which would impact defense contractors and military service providers.

bill.plainSummary: This bill would create a new procedural rule in the Senate to block the use of reconciliation—a fast-track budget process that avoids filibusters—for funding military operations against Iran unless Congress has formally declared war or passed a specific authorization. The rule could be overridden only by a 60-vote supermajority. In practice, it would make it harder to fund hostilities with Iran through budget bills that normally require only a simple majority.

plain.whoItTouches: Anyone who pays tax or gets a federal payment.

bill.title: A joint resolution to direct the removal of United States Armed Forces from hostilities that have not been authorized by Congress.
bill.latestActionText: Referred to the House Committee on Foreign Affairs.

industries.rationale: The resolution would restrict deployment of U.S. Armed Forces in certain overseas operations, directly affecting defense contractors and military service providers.

bill.plainSummary: This resolution would require the President to withdraw U.S. military forces from combat operations against terrorist organizations designated after February 20, 2025, or against drug-trafficking groups, unless Congress has formally declared war or authorized the use of force. The measure would still allow military action to defend against actual or imminent attacks and would permit armed forces to support domestic law enforcement in authorized anti-drug operations.

plain.whoItTouches: Mostly people outside the United States. It reaches most readers here only indirectly.

bill.title: Proposing an amendment to the Constitution of the United States relating to contributions and expenditures intended to affect elections.
bill.latestActionText: Referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary.

industries.rationale: Campaign finance regulation directly affects lobbying firms and election-law practitioners who advise on contribution and expenditure compliance.
Advocacy organizations that spend money on election-related communications would face new regulatory constraints on their expenditures.
Limits on campaign spending could affect demand for political advertising across broadcast, digital, and print media platforms.
Financial institutions that make political expenditures or operate PACs could face new restrictions on corporate election spending.

bill.plainSummary: This joint resolution proposes a constitutional amendment that would allow Congress and state governments to set limits on how much money candidates and others can raise and spend to influence elections. It would also permit lawmakers to treat corporations and other legal entities differently from individual people, including by banning corporate spending on elections. The amendment would require ratification by the states to take effect.

Regulations on election-related spending could affect advertising revenue and the market for political communications services.

bill.plainSummary: This proposed constitutional amendment would allow Congress and state legislatures to set limits on how much money candidates and others can raise and spend to influence elections. It would also permit them to create public financing systems for campaigns and to treat corporations differently from individual people, including by prohibiting corporations from spending money on elections. The amendment would give lawmakers the authority to write laws implementing these changes.

bill.title: To authorize judicial review of temporary protected status terminations, and for other purposes.
bill.latestActionText: Referred to the Committee on the Judiciary, and in addition to the Committee on Rules, for a period to be subsequently determined by the Speaker, in each case for consideration of such provisions as fall within the jurisdiction of the committee concerned.

industries.rationale: The bill creates new opportunities for judicial review, which would generate litigation work for immigration attorneys.
Agricultural employers rely on TPS holders as workers; changes to termination procedures could affect labor availability in this sector.
Hotels and restaurants employ TPS holders; judicial review of terminations could affect workforce stability in these industries.
Construction employers use TPS holders as workers; the bill's review mechanism could affect labor supply predictability.

bill.plainSummary: This bill would allow people to challenge in court when the government ends Temporary Protected Status (TPS) for their country. TPS is a designation that lets people from certain countries stay in the U.S. temporarily when their home country faces armed conflict, natural disaster, or other extraordinary conditions. Currently, decisions to terminate TPS are not subject to judicial review; this bill would change that.

bill.title: Accelerating Access to Critical Therapies for ALS Reauthorization Act of 2026
bill.latestActionText: Received in the Senate. Read twice. Placed on Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders. Calendar No. 466.
subjects: Department of Health and Human Services

industries.rationale: The bill directly funds research grants and regulatory pathways for development of drugs and therapies targeting ALS and neurodegenerative diseases.
Providers treating ALS patients may see changes in available investigational therapies and clinical trial access, though the bill focuses primarily on research and regulatory processes.

bill.plainSummary: This bill extends funding through fiscal year 2031 for federal programs that support research and development of treatments for ALS (Lou Gehrig's disease) and similar neurodegenerative diseases. It requires the National Institutes of Health to track safety data on experimental drugs and mandates that the Food and Drug Administration publish a five-year plan describing how it will help develop and approve therapies for these rare diseases. The bill also continues a public-private partnership between federal agencies and outside organizations working on neurodegenerative disease treatments.

plain.whoItTouches: People with an illness that is still being studied. Anyone who uses the internet.

bill.latestActionText: Referred to the Committee on Oversight and Government Reform, and in addition to the Committees on Rules, Armed Services, the Judiciary, and Energy and Commerce, for a period to be subsequently determined by the Speaker, in each case for consideration of such provisions as fall within the jurisdiction of the committee concerned.
subjects: Presidents and presidential powers, Vice Presidents

industries.rationale: The bill fundamentally restructures the governance of the District, creating a new state government and redefining the federal district.
Statehood would change property tax authority and land-use regulation for most of the current District, affecting developers and property owners.
The transition of DC courts, judicial proceedings, and contractual obligations to state authority would affect legal practice and litigation in the new jurisdiction.

bill.plainSummary: This bill would admit most of the current District of Columbia as the 51st state, called Washington, Douglass Commonwealth, with two senators and one representative in Congress. A small federal district containing the Capitol, White House, Supreme Court, and nearby monuments would remain as the seat of the federal government. The bill sets up a transition process for DC laws, courts, contracts, and obligations to continue under state authority, and creates a commission to manage the shift to statehood.

bill.title: Federal Extreme Risk Protection Order Act of 2026
bill.latestActionText: Referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary.

industries.rationale: The bill directly restricts firearm sales and possession for individuals subject to extreme risk orders, affecting manufacturers and dealers.
Advocacy organizations focused on gun rights, gun safety, and civil liberties have direct stakes in extreme risk protection order legislation.
The bill creates new federal court petition procedures and legal processes for contesting orders, generating demand for legal representation.

bill.plainSummary: This bill would allow family members and law enforcement to ask federal courts to temporarily prohibit someone from buying or possessing firearms if that person poses a danger to themselves or others. It would make it a federal crime for individuals subject to these orders to have guns, require the FBI to track such orders nationwide, and provide grants to help states and tribes create or enforce similar laws. The bill sets out procedures for issuing, contesting, and renewing these temporary restrictions.

bill.title: Scientific Integrity Act
bill.latestActionText: Referred to the House Committee on Science, Space, and Technology.

industries.rationale: Pharmaceutical and biotech companies conduct and rely on federally funded research subject to these integrity requirements.
Federal research on climate, emissions, and energy impacts this sector's regulatory environment and public discourse.
Federal research on energy technologies and climate directly affects this sector's market and policy landscape.
Agricultural research conducted or funded by USDA and other agencies would be subject to these integrity standards.
Universities receive federal research funding and would need to comply with integrity policies in their federally supported work.

bill.plainSummary: This bill would require every federal agency that funds, conducts, or oversees scientific research to create and enforce a policy protecting scientific integrity. These policies must ensure that research conclusions are not influenced by political considerations, prohibit suppression or alteration of findings, and allow researchers to share their work. Each agency would need to appoint a Scientific Integrity Officer, establish a complaint process, provide training, and submit its policy to the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy for approval.
